status: proposed coverage; availability comes from authored lesson files
lessonStandard: Each lesson needs original explanatory sections, defined quantities and restrictions, at least two reasoned worked examples, a guided multi-part task, misconception feedback, a prediction-led investigation with keyboard inputs and an equivalent table, at least eight practice slots across distinct families, four checkpoint slots, a recall task, and verified reading links. The examples below are authoring specifications, not completed lessons.

lessons.title: Units, dimensions, and measurement evidence
lessons.objective: Convert mechanical quantities consistently, test dimensional homogeneity, and interpret a measurement with a stated uncertainty model.
topics: SI base and derived units; mass versus weight
prefixes on squared and cubed units
dimensions of coefficients in time-dependent models
dimensional consistency as a necessary but insufficient model check
instrument resolution versus accuracy and repeatability
bounded uncertainty and independent random uncertainty distinguished
examples: Convert a small cross-sectional area before calculating stress; check the conversion by reversing it.
Bound speed from measured distance and duration with interval endpoints; explain why agreement within uncertainty does not prove a model.
lessons.investigation: Vary distance, time, and their nonnegative absolute uncertainty bounds; predict the effect of doubled resolution and reveal central speed and worst-case bounds. Reject intervals containing nonpositive elapsed time. The output table supplies units and assumptions.
criticalChecks: Square the prefix conversion factor for area.
Do not add unlike dimensions.
Distinguish a bound from a standard deviation.

lessons.title: Vectors in a right-handed coordinate system
lessons.objective: Resolve and combine three-dimensional vectors and distinguish projections, dot products, and cross products with their directions and units.
topics: position versus displacement; vector versus scalar
Cartesian components and unit vectors in 2D and 3D
cross product components, right-hand rule, and antisymmetry
examples: A sensor moves between two 3D coordinates: calculate displacement, length, and a unit direction.
Use the same two vectors to calculate a scalar projection and a torque-like cross product; check perpendicularity.
lessons.investigation: Edit two vectors, predict their sum and product signs, and switch their order. Compare component tables and a labeled planar projection; explicitly distinguish projected length from full 3D length.
criticalChecks: A magnitude cannot be negative.
A zero vector has no unique direction.
Reversing cross-product order reverses its sign.

lessons.title: Position, velocity, acceleration, and graphs
lessons.objective: Connect one-dimensional motion functions and graphs using derivatives and definite integrals, including reversals and initial conditions.
examples: Differentiate a cubic position and identify when slowing changes to speeding.
Integrate an affine acceleration with nonzero initial position and velocity, then split distance at a reversal.
lessons.investigation: Change initial velocity and acceleration and predict a turning time. Show synchronized position, velocity, and acceleration samples and signed interval areas.
criticalChecks: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing.
Velocity zero does not imply acceleration zero.
Displacement and distance differ at a reversal.

lessons.title: Motion and relative velocity in three dimensions
lessons.objective: Differentiate vector trajectories and transform relative positions and velocities between stated inertial frames.
topics: horizontal and vertical independence only when forces permit
examples: Differentiate a three-component trajectory at a supplied time and calculate speed.
Recover ground velocity from a vehicle velocity relative to a moving platform; reverse the observer convention.
lessons.investigation: Vary observer velocity and compare position and velocity component tables in both frames. Test that common acceleration is unchanged under a constant-velocity frame change.
criticalChecks: State which object is relative to which observer.
Differentiate components before taking the norm.

lessons.title: Projectile motion and admissible flight times
lessons.objective: Model a projectile with vector initial conditions, select physically admissible roots, and explain the limits of the constant-gravity approximation.
topics: positive flight time and model interval
maximum height with nonzero horizontal speed
examples: Launch from a raised platform and solve for landing time and horizontal displacement.
Find an apex and explain why the velocity vector remains nonzero.
lessons.investigation: Change launch components and height, predict landing time, and compare a trajectory plot with time-position tables. Stop the displayed flight at its first admissible ground impact.
criticalChecks: Do not accept negative time as a future landing.
The apex has zero vertical velocity, not zero acceleration.

lessons.title: Free-body diagrams and Newton's laws
lessons.objective: Choose a system, identify external interactions, and solve signed component equations for its acceleration or support forces.
topics: inertial frames and net external force
normal and tension as constraint forces
third-law pairs act on different bodies
examples: Solve an accelerating lift's scale reading and examine free fall.
Resolve gravity and a pull on a frictionless incline; check the normal direction.
lessons.investigation: Toggle applied forces on a single chosen body, predict component acceleration, and inspect a force inventory and resultant table.
criticalChecks: Do not include both members of a third-law pair on one body.
A normal force need not equal weight.

lessons.title: Static friction and connected bodies
lessons.objective: Determine whether sticking is possible, choose the appropriate friction model, and solve coupled equations with consistent constraints.
topics: massless inextensible rope and ideal pulley limits
contact loss and impossible normal forces
examples: Increase a horizontal pull through the static threshold and compare sliding acceleration.
Model two connected masses; eliminate internal tension using a whole-system equation.
lessons.investigation: Change load and friction coefficients and predict rest or sliding before revealing force components. Compare a force just below, at, and above the threshold.
criticalChecks: Static friction is not always its maximum.
Negative required normal force means contact assumptions failed.

lessons.title: Velocity-dependent drag and terminal motion
lessons.objective: Form and check a linear-drag differential equation, interpret its time constant, and distinguish terminal motion from free fall.
topics: linear drag and quadratic drag domains
separation or verification of exponential solution
initial conditions and time constant m/b
examples: Derive vertical speed from rest with downward positive and linear drag.
Check a proposed terminal speed using force balance and dimensional analysis.
lessons.investigation: Vary mass and drag coefficient and compare dimensionless time t/(m/b), predicted terminal speed, and tabulated residual acceleration.
criticalChecks: Terminal velocity is not zero velocity.
The linear-drag formula does not apply at b=0 without taking a limit.

lessons.title: Uniform and nonuniform circular motion
lessons.objective: Separate radial and tangential acceleration and use actual forces to sustain a circular path with constant or changing speed.
topics: loss of contact; centripetal names a resultant
examples: Find total acceleration for a rotor whose speed increases.
Compute top-of-loop contact force and minimum speed under a unilateral contact model.
lessons.investigation: Vary radius, speed, and tangential acceleration, predicting which components change and whether contact is possible; show a vector-component table.
criticalChecks: Do not add a fictitious extra centripetal force to the free-body diagram.
Constant speed can coexist with nonzero acceleration.

lessons.title: Gravity, orbits, and Newton's synthesis
lessons.objective: Relate inverse-square gravity to near-surface weight, circular orbital motion, escape energy, and Kepler's scaling laws.
topics: superposition and limits of circular formulas
examples: Compare gravitational acceleration at two center distances and derive circular period.
Compare escape and orbital speeds, stating the zero of potential at infinity.
lessons.investigation: Scale orbital radius and predict g, speed, and period ratios; compare calculated ratios to r squared and r cubed laws in a table.
criticalChecks: Altitude is not the center distance.
Apparent weightlessness does not mean no gravity.

lessons.title: Work as a vector line integral
lessons.objective: Calculate signed work for constant and position-dependent forces and verify it against kinetic-energy change.
topics: net work and kinetic energy theorem derivation
examples: Integrate a position-dependent force over a bounded interval.
Calculate work by a nonparallel force and use independent acceleration kinematics to check kinetic-energy change.
lessons.investigation: Change a force's angle or position slope and compare a prediction with work-area tables and kinetic-energy change.
criticalChecks: Work can be negative; kinetic energy cannot.
Force times path length requires a constant parallel force.

lessons.title: Energy systems, potential, and efficiency
lessons.objective: Choose a system boundary, account for potential and dissipated energy, and determine reachable states and power requirements.
topics: conservative force and negative potential gradient
examples: A spring launches a cart up a rough ramp: include thermal energy and solve a stopping condition.
Read equilibrium and accessible regions from a simple potential function.
lessons.investigation: Change initial energy and dissipation, predict whether a barrier is reachable, and inspect a complete energy ledger.
criticalChecks: Do not assume mechanical energy conservation with friction.
A negative computed speed squared signals an unreachable state.

lessons.title: Impulse and center-of-mass motion
lessons.objective: Integrate force to obtain impulse and use a system's external impulse to predict total momentum and center-of-mass motion.
topics: center of mass for discrete and continuous distributions
examples: Integrate a triangular force pulse and predict final signed velocity.
Locate the center of mass of three particles and determine its acceleration from external force.
lessons.investigation: Keep impulse fixed while changing pulse duration; predict peak force and compare a force-time table and momentum ledger.
criticalChecks: Zero external impulse is the momentum conservation condition.
Internal forces can change individual momenta.

lessons.title: Collisions and explosions in multiple dimensions
lessons.objective: Apply vector momentum conservation to collisions or separation events and audit kinetic energy before selecting an elastic model.
examples: Two objects stick after approaching along different axes; find velocity and energy loss.
Solve a one-dimensional elastic collision and verify both conserved totals.
lessons.investigation: Vary masses and incoming velocities; compare elastic and sticking outcomes using momentum and energy tables.
criticalChecks: Momentum conservation alone does not conserve kinetic energy.
Conserve each component, not the sum of speed magnitudes.

lessons.title: Angular motion, torque, and rotational inertia
lessons.objective: Relate angular and tangential variables, calculate torque about a stated axis, and derive or combine moments of inertia.
topics: torque cross product and lever arm
I as sum or integral of squared radius
net torque equals I alpha for a fixed axis
examples: Compute a three-dimensional torque and its component about the allowed axis.
Integrate the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about its center and check an end-axis result.
lessons.investigation: Move point masses radially and predict inertia and angular acceleration for fixed torque; show contributions to I in a table.
criticalChecks: Torque uses perpendicular distance.
Moment of inertia depends on the selected axis.

lessons.title: Angular momentum and rotational work
lessons.objective: Use external torque and angular impulse to track angular momentum and distinguish its conservation from energy conservation.
topics: work integral torque dtheta and power
changing inertia with conserved angular momentum
examples: A spinning system pulls masses inward: compare final speed and energy supplied.
A particle strikes and sticks to a rotor: conserve angular momentum about the fixed axle and calculate energy loss.
lessons.investigation: Change inertia under either fixed angular momentum or fixed angular speed; predict the energy response and inspect the work needed.
criticalChecks: Conserved angular momentum need not imply conserved kinetic energy.
Name the origin and axis used for the torque balance.

lessons.title: Rolling constraints and coupled translation
lessons.objective: Solve rolling motion using translation, rotation, and a verified no-slip constraint, including the required static friction.
topics: v equals omega R only without slip
rolling versus sliding and model failure
examples: Derive a solid cylinder's acceleration down a ramp and required friction.
Compare a hoop and a sphere released from the same height using energy and dynamics.
lessons.investigation: Change inertia ratio and incline angle; predict acceleration and test no-slip feasibility against a friction limit.
criticalChecks: Do not impose rolling if the needed friction exceeds its bound.
Include both translational and rotational energy.

lessons.title: Static equilibrium and support reactions
lessons.objective: Solve force and torque equilibrium for a rigid body and assess support, contact, and tipping constraints.
topics: zero net force and torque are both needed
examples: Find two supports' reactions for a weighted beam with an off-center load.
Determine a tipping threshold and explain the zero reaction at the lifting support.
lessons.investigation: Move a load along a beam; predict support trends and identify when a unilateral reaction would be impossible.
criticalChecks: Force balance alone does not establish equilibrium.
A support that can only push cannot supply negative reaction.

lessons.title: Stress, strain, and elastic response
lessons.objective: Relate tensile, shear, and bulk stress to deformation within a stated linear elastic regime and propagate measurement limits.
topics: stress versus force and strain versus extension
examples: Predict wire extension and energy from load, area, length, and modulus.
Calculate volume change under a pressure increment with a stated bulk modulus.
lessons.investigation: Vary length and cross-sectional area, predict compliance changes, and compare stress/strain tables only inside the declared linear range.
criticalChecks: Convert squared millimeters correctly.
Modulus has pressure units; strain is dimensionless.

lessons.title: Plasticity, fracture, and evidence limits
lessons.objective: Interpret a stress-strain record and distinguish stiffness, yielding, strength, toughness, and the limitations of a simple failure estimate.
topics: stress-strain area as energy per volume
safety-factor calculations as supplied classroom models
examples: Integrate a piecewise linear stress-strain curve to compare two hypothetical materials.
Audit a supplied allowable-stress calculation and explain why it is not certification of a structure.
lessons.investigation: Compare synthetic stress-strain tables with equal initial slopes and different failure strains; predict which is tougher and explain what the plot cannot establish.
criticalChecks: Stiffness and strength are different properties.
Do not extrapolate Hooke's law beyond the stated elastic range.
No home breaking, tensioning, or pressure experiment is assigned.

lessons.title: Numerical integration and convergence evidence
lessons.objective: Implement bounded time steps, compare numerical methods with an analytic case, and distinguish discretization error from model and measurement error.
topics: energy residuals without false conservation claims
examples: Integrate irregular velocity samples and check units and signed area.
Compare Euler position against exact constant-acceleration motion at h, h/2, and h/4.
lessons.investigation: Choose step size and method for an idealized mass-spring system; predict drift and compare time, position, velocity, and energy residuals in a downloadable table.
criticalChecks: Update ordering defines the algorithm.
Smaller steps cannot repair the wrong physical model.

lessons.title: Validate a mechanical subsystem
lessons.objective: Combine force, energy, numerical, and measurement evidence into a reproducible investigation with a transparent self-assessment rubric.
topics: reproducible simulated data versus physical observations
examples: Validate an idealized cart-spring subsystem against analytic energy and period predictions, treating oscillations only as a model-checking application.
Diagnose a simulation that gains energy because of its integration scheme, then distinguish this from damping in recorded physical motion.
lessons.investigation: Complete the project notebook with model assumptions, predictions, a convergence table, a controlled comparison, a residual explanation, and a revision. Save locally and restore through the normal backup.
criticalChecks: Label all data provenance.
Self-assessment does not count as independent subject review.
A good fit cannot establish every model assumption.
